title: Spherical Waves
short_intro: Spherical waves are three-dimensional mechanical or electromagnetic waves where wavefronts form concentric spheres originating from a point source. Their amplitude decreases inversely with distance from the source to conserve total radiated energy.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of spherical wavefronts, inverse-square law for intensity, and relation between amplitude and distance from a point source.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation of the three-dimensional scalar wave equation in spherical polar coordinates and its divergent wave solutions of the form Psi(r,t) = (A/r)cos(kr - omega t).

prerequisites: Simple harmonic motion and wave kinematics
Vector calculus and spherical polar coordinate systems

concept_notes.heading: Wavefronts and Rays in Three Dimensions
bullets: A wavefront is the locus of all adjacent points vibrating in the same phase, forming concentric spheres for a point source.
Wave normals (rays) point radially outward, indicating the direction of energy propagation.
As the radius r of the wavefront increases, the local surface area of the sphere grows as 4πr<sup>2</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Amplitude Variation with Distance
bullets: Total wave power P crossing any spherical surface of radius r remains constant in a lossless medium.
Since intensity I is power per unit area, I = P / (4πr<sup>2</sup>), meaning intensity varies inversely as r<sup>2</sup>.
Because wave intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude (I ∝ A<sup>2</sup>), the displacement amplitude A must vary inversely with distance r: A(r) = A<sub>0</sub> / r.

concept_notes.heading: The 3D Wave Equation in Spherical Coordinates
bullets: In regions devoid of sources and assuming spherical symmetry, the scalar wave equation depends only on the radial coordinate r and time t.
The Laplacian operator in spherical coordinates reduces to (1/r<sup>2</sup>) ∂/∂r(r<sup>2</sup> ∂/∂r).
The differential equation takes the form ∂<sup>2</sup>(rΨ)/∂t<sup>2</sup> = v<sup>2</sup> ∂<sup>2</sup>(rΨ)/∂r<sup>2</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Energy Transport and Intensity
bullets: The average intensity of a spherical wave is given by I<sub>avg</sub> = 2π<sup>2</sup> ρ v f<sup>2</sup> A<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> / r<sup>2</sup>.
Spherical waves attenuate purely due to geometric spreading, independent of medium absorption (which causes exponential damping).
At distances very large compared to the source dimensions, spherical wavefronts can be approximated locally as planar wavefronts.

derivations.title: Derivation of Spherical Wave Equation Solution
derivations.conditions: Homogeneous, isotropic, lossless medium with spherical symmetry
steps: Write the three-dimensional scalar wave equation: ∇<sup>2</sup>Ψ = (1/v<sup>2</sup>)(∂<sup>2</sup>Ψ/∂t<sup>2</sup>).
Expand the Laplacian for spherically symmetric fields where Ψ = Ψ(r,t): (1/r<sup>2</sup>)∂/∂r(r<sup>2</sup> ∂Ψ/∂r) = (1/v<sup>2</sup>)(∂<sup>2</sup>Ψ/∂t<sup>2</sup>).
Substitute u(r,t) = rΨ(r,t). Then ∂Ψ/∂r = (1/r)(∂u/∂r - u/r), leading to ∂<sup>2</sup>u/∂r<sup>2</sup> = (1/v<sup>2</sup>)(∂<sup>2</sup>u/∂t<sup>2</sup>).
Solve the resulting 1D wave equation for u: u(r,t) = f(r - vt) + g(r + vt).
Divide by r to obtain the spherical wave solution: Ψ(r,t) = (1/r)f(r - vt).

derivations.title: Derivation of Inverse Square Law for Intensity
derivations.conditions: Isotropic point source emitting constant average power P in a non-absorbing medium
steps: Consider a point source emitting power P uniformly in all directions.
Enclose the source with an imaginary sphere of radius r. The total surface area of this sphere is S = 4\pi r^2.
Define intensity I as the power per unit area: I = \frac{P}{S} = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2}.
Express wave intensity in terms of displacement amplitude A: I = \frac{1}{2} \rho v \omega^2 A^2.
Equate the two expressions to show A^2 \propto \frac{1}{r^2}, yielding A \propto \frac{1}{r}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wavefronts and Rays
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Concentric circles drawn around a central point source with orthogonal radial arrows pointing outwards labeled as rays.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that wavefronts are spherical surfaces expanding outward, while rays indicate the direction of energy transport perpendicular to wavefronts.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding the geometrical relationship between wavefronts and rays.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Amplitude vs Distance (A vs r)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola curve plotting displacement amplitude A on the vertical axis against radial distance r on the horizontal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the inverse relationship A ∝ 1/r, showing rapid drop-off near the source and gradual leveling further away.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to interpret numerical scaling problems where distance is doubled or tripled.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs Inverse Square Distance (I vs 1/r^2)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin with a positive slope representing intensity I plotted against 1/r^2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms the inverse-square law of wave intensity for a point source in a 3D medium.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in graphical analysis questions in PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: If the amplitude of a spherical wave is 5.0 cm at a distance of 2.0 m from a point source, what is the amplitude at a distance of 10.0 m?
solution_steps: Identify the inverse proportionality between amplitude and distance for a spherical wave: A_1 r_1 = A_2 r_2.
Substitute the given values: A_1 = 5.0 cm, r_1 = 2.0 m, r_2 = 10.0 m.
Calculate the final value: A_2 = 10 / 10 = 1.0 cm.

solved_numericals.question: A small acoustic point source radiates sound power uniformly at 31.4 W in an open field. Calculate the sound intensity and the displacement amplitude of air particles at a distance of 5.0 m. Take density of air ρ = 1.2 kg/m^3, speed of sound v = 340 m/s, and frequency f = 500 Hz.
solution_steps: Relate intensity to amplitude using I = (1/2) ρ v ω^2 A^2, where ω = 2πf = 2 * 3.1416 * 500 = 3141.6 rad/s.
Rearrange for amplitude A: A = sqrt(2I / (ρ v ω^2)).

solved_numericals.question: At what distance from an isotropic point source does the intensity of a spherical wave drop to 1/9th of its value at 3.0 m?
solution_steps: Recall the inverse square law: I ∝ 1/r^2, which implies I_1 / I_2 = (r_2 / r_1)^2.
Given I_2 = (1/9) I_1, substitute this ratio into the equation: 9 = (r_2 / 3.0)^2.
Take the square root on both sides: r_2 / 3.0 = 3.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the medium is homogeneous, isotropic, and infinite, neglecting boundary reflections and refraction.
Assumes a point source of zero physical dimensions; real sources have finite sizes where near-field deviations occur.
Does not account for attenuation due to medium absorption or scattering, which introduces an exponential damping factor e^{-\alpha r}.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Spherical wave intensity is inversely proportional to distance r.
common_misconceptions.correct: Intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance (r^2).
common_misconceptions.why: Energy spreads over the surface area of a sphere, which grows as 4πr^2, not its radius.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Frequency of a spherical wave changes as it propagates outward.
common_misconceptions.correct: Frequency remains constant and depends solely on the source.
common_misconceptions.why: Wave propagation through a stationary, linear medium alters amplitude and phase, but not frequency.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Spherical waves can only exist in three dimensions for sound.
common_misconceptions.correct: Spherical waves occur in any three-dimensional isotropic medium, including light, sound, and seismic waves.
common_misconceptions.why: The geometric requirement of 1/r amplitude dependence arises purely from 3D divergence of wavefronts.

quick_revision: Spherical wavefronts emerge from point sources and expand with surface area 4πr^2.
Displacement amplitude decays as A(r) = A_0 / r.
Wave intensity obeys the inverse square law I = P / (4πr^2).
The 3D scalar wave equation reduces to a 1D wave equation via the substitution u = rΨ.
